objectives: Trace the discovery of circulation from Galen through Harvey, Frank, Starling, Einthoven, and Forssmann.
Read the cardiac pressure-volume loop and identify its four phases and two valve events.
Define preload, afterload, contractility, stroke volume, and ejection fraction quantitatively.

slides.title: How we learned the heart is a pump
slides.body:
For 1,400 years European medicine followed **Galen of Pergamon** (c. 129-216 CE), who taught that the liver continuously manufactured blood from food, that blood ebbed and flowed like a tide through invisible pores in the interventricular septum, and that it was consumed by the tissues. This was wrong in almost every particular, but it was authoritative.

The correction came in stages. **Ibn al-Nafis** (1213-1288), working in Damascus and Cairo, described the **pulmonary circuit** in the 13th century, denying Galen's septal pores and insisting blood must pass through the lungs. In Renaissance Europe, **Andreas Vesalius** (1514-1564) overturned Galenic anatomy through dissection in his 1543 *De humani corporis fabrica*, and **Michael Servetus** and **Realdo Colombo** independently rediscovered the pulmonary transit in the 1550s.

The decisive synthesis was **William Harvey** (1578-1657). In his 1628 treatise *Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus*, Harvey argued from quantity: he estimated the volume ejected per beat, multiplied by heart rate, and showed the heart pumps far more blood per hour than the body weighs, so the blood **cannot** be consumed — it must **circulate** in a closed loop. This is arguably the first quantitative physiological argument in history. Harvey could not see the connection between arteries and veins; the missing link, the **capillaries**, was supplied by **Marcello Malpighi** in 1661 using the new microscope.

The modern era of cardiac mechanics opens with two physiologists. **Otto Frank** (1865-1944) published in 1895 on how the isolated frog heart responds to filling. **Ernest Starling** (1866-1927), with his dog heart-lung preparation, formalized in 1918 what we now call the **Frank-Starling law of the heart**: within limits, the more the ventricle is filled during diastole, the more forcefully it contracts and the greater the stroke volume. Greater **preload** stretches the myocardium and increases the force of the next contraction.

Two more pillars complete the foundation. **Willem Einthoven** (1860-1927) invented the practical string galvanometer electrocardiograph around 1901-1903, winning the **Nobel Prize in 1924** and giving us the P, QRS, and T waves we still read. **Werner Forssmann** (1904-1979) in 1929 threaded a catheter through a vein in his own arm into his right atrium, founding **cardiac catheterization**; he shared the **Nobel Prize in 1956** with Andre Cournand and Dickinson Richards. By the mid-20th century, the heart was understood as a measurable, instrumentable pump.

slides.title: Reading the pressure-volume loop
slides.body:
The single most informative picture in cardiac mechanics is the **left-ventricular pressure-volume (PV) loop**, plotting intraventricular **pressure** (vertical, mmHg) against **volume** (horizontal, mL) over one heartbeat. The loop is traced counterclockwise and has four phases bounded by the opening and closing of two valves.

Start at the bottom-right corner, at **end-diastolic volume (EDV)**, typically about 120 mL.

- **1. Isovolumetric contraction.** Both the **mitral valve** and the **aortic valve** are shut. The ventricle contracts, so pressure climbs steeply while volume is fixed — a vertical line up the right edge. This phase ends when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg) and the aortic valve snaps open.
- **2. Ejection.** The aortic valve is open. Blood is ejected into the aorta, so volume falls while pressure first rises then declines — the top of the loop, moving leftward. It ends at **end-systolic volume (ESV)**, typically about 50 mL, when the aortic valve closes.
- **3. Isovolumetric relaxation.** Both valves shut again. The ventricle relaxes, pressure plummets at constant (low) volume — a vertical line down the left edge. It ends when ventricular pressure falls below left-atrial pressure and the mitral valve opens.
- **4. Filling.** The mitral valve is open. Blood flows in from the left atrium; volume rises along the bottom of the loop back to EDV, with only a small pressure increase.

The **width** of the loop is the **stroke volume**: $SV = EDV - ESV \approx 120 - 50 = 70$ mL. The **area enclosed** by the loop equals the **stroke work** done by the ventricle on the blood.

Two boundary lines frame the loop. The lower-right curve is the **end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship (EDPVR)**, reflecting passive ventricular **compliance** (a stiff ventricle bows upward). The upper-left line is the **end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR)**; its slope, $E_{es}$, is a load-independent index of **contractility** named by **Hiroyuki Suga** and **Kiichi Sagawa** in the 1970s. Increasing contractility rotates the ESPVR steeper and counterclockwise, shrinking ESV and widening the loop. This single diagram lets us read preload (where filling stops), afterload (the pressure at which ejection begins), and contractility (the ESPVR slope) all at once.

slides.title: Preload, afterload, contractility, and ejection fraction
slides.body:
Four interlocking concepts govern how much blood the heart moves. Confusing them is the most common error of beginning students, so define each precisely.

**Preload** is the load on the myocardium *before* it contracts — the degree of stretch of the sarcomeres at end-diastole. Operationally it is indexed by **end-diastolic volume (EDV)** or by filling pressures such as **left-ventricular end-diastolic pressure (LVEDP)** or the **pulmonary capillary wedge pressure**. By the **Frank-Starling mechanism**, raising preload (more venous return, a larger blood volume) increases stroke volume — up to a point, beyond which an overstretched, failing ventricle plateaus or declines.

**Afterload** is the load the ventricle must work *against* during ejection — essentially the wall stress required to open the aortic valve and push blood into the systemic circulation. It rises with **arterial blood pressure**, with aortic stiffness, and with **aortic stenosis**. Wall stress is captured by the **law of Laplace**: for a thin-walled sphere, $\sigma = \frac{P \cdot r}{2h}$, where $P$ is pressure, $r$ is chamber radius, and $h$ is wall thickness. A dilated ventricle (large $r$) faces higher wall stress for the same pressure, which is why dilation begets further dysfunction.

**Contractility** (inotropy) is the intrinsic vigor of contraction *independent* of preload and afterload. It is increased by sympathetic stimulation, **catecholamines** (epinephrine, norepinephrine), and drugs such as **digoxin** and **dobutamine**; it is the slope $E_{es}$ of the ESPVR. Crucially, contractility changes are separate from Frank-Starling changes: Starling alters force by changing fiber length, whereas inotropy alters force *at a fixed length*.

**Stroke volume (SV)** is the blood ejected per beat, $SV = EDV - ESV$, typically about 70 mL. It rises with increased preload or contractility and falls with increased afterload.

**Ejection fraction (EF)** is the *fraction* of end-diastolic volume ejected:

$$EF = \frac{SV}{EDV} = \frac{EDV - ESV}{EDV} \times 100\%$$

A normal left-ventricular EF is roughly **55-70%**. With $EDV = 120$ mL and $ESV = 50$ mL, $EF = 70/120 \approx 58\%$. EF is the workhorse clinical measure of systolic function: a reduced EF (below ~40%) defines **heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF)**, whereas heart failure can also occur with preserved EF (**HFpEF**) when the ventricle is stiff and fills poorly. Cardiac output ties it together: $CO = HR \times SV$, so a resting heart at 70 bpm with 70 mL strokes pumps about 4.9 L/min.

question.question: On the left-ventricular pressure-volume loop, during which phase are BOTH the mitral and aortic valves closed while pressure rises sharply?
question.explanation: Isovolumetric contraction occurs after the mitral valve closes but before the aortic valve opens. With both valves shut, the contracting ventricle raises pressure at constant volume — the vertical right edge of the loop. Ejection requires the aortic valve open; filling requires the mitral valve open; isovolumetric relaxation also has both valves shut but pressure falls.

hints: Pressure is rising, so the ventricle is contracting, not relaxing.
If volume is unchanged, no blood is leaving or entering, so neither valve is open.
slides.workedSolution: Both valves shut + pressure rising = isovolumetric contraction (the right vertical limb). It ends the instant LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure and the aortic valve opens, beginning ejection.

question.question: A left ventricle has an end-diastolic volume of 130 mL and an end-systolic volume of 52 mL. Compute the stroke volume in mL.
question.hint: Stroke volume is end-diastolic volume minus end-systolic volume: SV = EDV - ESV.

question.question: Using EDV = 130 mL and ESV = 52 mL, compute the ejection fraction as a percentage, rounded to the nearest whole percent.
question.hint: EF = SV / EDV * 100%. With SV = 78 mL and EDV = 130 mL, divide and multiply by 100.

question.question: A runner's heart at the moment of a sprint
question.prompt: During a sudden sprint, an athlete's sympathetic nervous system floods the heart with norepinephrine, the heart rate climbs from 60 to 170 bpm, and venous return rises sharply as leg muscles squeeze blood back to the heart. Explain, in terms of preload and contractility, how the pressure-volume loop changes shape: which way does the end-systolic pressure-volume relationship (ESPVR) rotate, what happens to end-systolic volume, and why does stroke volume increase even though filling time per beat is shorter? Relate your reasoning to the Frank-Starling mechanism and to the contractility slope E_es.

question.question: Which historical figure first argued, using quantitative reasoning about volume per beat times heart rate, that blood must circulate in a closed loop rather than be consumed by the tissues?
question.explanation: William Harvey, in De Motu Cordis (1628), reasoned that the heart pumps more blood per hour than the body weighs, so blood cannot be continuously made and consumed (Galen's view) but must circulate. Einthoven invented the ECG (Nobel 1924) and Forssmann pioneered cardiac catheterization (Nobel 1956) — both centuries later.

hints: The key date is 1628 and the key idea is a closed loop.
Galen held the consumption theory that this person overturned.
slides.workedSolution: Harvey's quantitative argument — stroke volume times beats per hour vastly exceeds body weight — disproved Galen's consumption model and established circulation. Malpighi later (1661) found the capillaries that completed the loop.
